newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Back to work, Zaire rebels tell fallen Mbuji-Mayi.
newsitem.headline: Back to work, Zaire rebels tell fallen Mbuji-Mayi.

text.p: Residents cheered on Saturday after Zairean rebels took their town and said they wanted to get business back to normal at the diamond mines and on the streets of Mbuji-Mayi.

"They appeared on local television saying they wanted everything to get back to normal. They warned people they risked being shot if they looted," one mining source told Reuters by telephone from the city.
"They want the shops and schools to reopen on Monday."

Soldiers looted the Zairean diamond capital before fleeing on Friday and the rebels marched in without a fight to take their most important economic prize yet in the war to end the 32-year rule of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"People are cheering in the streets, there's a heck of a lot of noise. They are treating this as very good news," one mining source said.
He said local people estimated around 1,000 rebel soldiers were in the city, capital of Kasai province whose industrial quality diamonds are Zaire's main foreign currency earner.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila was expected to arrive in Mbuji- Mayi at the weekend and hold a rally on Monday in the football stadium.

Illegal diggers, profiting from the chaos during the city's capture, invaded the diamond mines of the part Belgian-owned MIBA concern which dominates the local economy to grab what they can before order is restored, the sources said.
The rebels stamped their authority on Mbuji-Mayi on Saturday -- just as peace talks with Mobutu's representatives began in South Africa.
As in other cities taken by Kabila's forces, the only reports of combat were between rival factions of Zaire's disintegrating army and not between army and rebels.
"Some people wounded by the military were brought in from the bush this morning," one source said.
He said rebels led by a General Mulufa had met the governor of Mbuji-Mayi and MIBA president Mukamba Kadiata Nzemba.
"We hope that when the negotiations are over the rebels will go in and clear the areas of the mines which have been invaded by illegal diggers," the mining source said.

Trouble began early on Friday in the city, some 1,000 km (600 miles) east of the capital Kinshasa and as far west of the second city Lubumbashi, when soldiers set up roadblocks and robbed people of vehicles, watches and money.
They started firing around town, shooting off locks of houses, shops, MIBA installations and the premises of Lebanese diamond buyers in the city -- many of whom had earlier fled.
"Some soldiers took off their uniforms, shot their way in here and robbed us," said the source.
"There was looting and shooting, they took all they could and then suddenly, at around two p.m., the soldiers left town. They made their escape in MIBA vehicles."
"Then local people, mostly youths, started to pillage. We were attacked with stones by a crowd of hooligans, I was hit on the head," he said.
There was no immediate official word on the biggest blow so far to the purse of Mobutu's authorities.
Rebels have now taken more than third of Zaire since October.
Mbuji-Mayi's fall has raised tension in Lubumbashi, which Kabila has vowed to take and which looks likely to be next.
